Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C using a regulator-approved protocol and a representative sample. A model passes if no more than 7% of tested units fail. The manufacturer must retain the complete per-model results and provide them to the relevant regulator on request and to an independent accredited testing body; results are not published as company-specific per-model failure rates. If a model fails, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan.

Manufacturers must report to the regulator and notify affected customers of any thermal incident involving fire, smoke, injury, hospitalization, evacuation, or property damage within 24 hours of learning of it. Other overheating incidents that require emergency intervention or cause a unit to shut down must be reported to the regulator within 5 business days and disclosed to affected customers within 10 business days. Reports must include the model, incident date and known circumstances; manufacturers must promptly supplement incomplete reports. Reporting obligations apply regardless of whether the incident is confirmed to be caused by the battery.

Results must not be withheld from customers as confidential. A model exceeding the limit may not be newly sold until it passes a retest, and the manufacturer must notify the regulator and affected customers and submit a corrective-action plan.

Before purchase, customers must receive the model’s per-model 55 °C sustained-heat test results, relevant safety instructions, known material risks, and instructions for reporting incidents. Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of safety incidents, corrective actions, and any changes to safe use; urgent hazards require notice within 24 hours of learning of them. A manufacturer must initiate a recall when a model’s confirmed thermal-incident rate exceeds 10 per 100,000 installed units in a year, or when the regulator determines that a defect presents an imminent serious risk. The manufacturer must provide the regulator with the data and analysis supporting its incident-rate calculation.

For transparency, Northwind’s Hearth 10 has a 6.2% failure rate at 55 °C and 6.4 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units last year; our company-wide rate was 8.6, with three incidents unreported to regulators. These figures support careful testing and reporting, but a 5% pass limit would exclude a model whose incident rate is below the discussed recall threshold. We propose a 7% maximum failure rate, with per-model results provided confidentially to regulators and accredited testing bodies.

All new home battery units placed on the market must support remote emergency shut-off within 24 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide safe, accessible shut-off instructions to customers and ensure the capability does not prevent emergency responders from isolating a system. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a retrofit or equivalent safe shut-off capability within 36 months where technically feasible, and disclose any limitations to affected customers.

Built-in fire suppression is required on all new home battery units placed on the market beginning 36 months after adoption. The suppression system must be suitable for the battery chemistry and installation environment and must be validated through independent safety testing. Manufacturers must provide customers and regulators with installation, maintenance, and operational instructions.
